implementation_notes: Rust has a first-party consumer crate: PactBuilder::new(consumer, provider).interaction("description", "", |mut i| { i.given(...); i.request.path(...); i.response.body(...); i }) declares one interaction and .start_mock_server(None, None) starts the mock server in-process; the returned MockServer lets the client under test be pointed at provider_service.path(...), and the pact is validated when the server value goes out of scope (the documented examples run under #[tokio::test] against reqwest). Matchers are macros - like!, each_like!, term!, json_pattern! - and message contracts need the V4 builder (PactBuilder::new_v4 with message_interaction or synchronous_message_interaction).
pitfalls: The mock server is the assertion point: the test fails only when the returned MockServer is dropped, so an early return or a mem::forget skips verification entirely.
The documented examples are async (tokio/reqwest): blocking on the client inside an async test deadlocks the runtime, and starting the mock server in a plain #[test] requires its own runtime.
Message and synchronous-message interactions require the V4 builder (new_v4); using the default builder produces request/response contracts that other implementations cannot read as message pacts.
